2. Cutaneous sarcoidosis — Can present as persistent reddish‑brown plaques on limbs/hip; consider especially if there are systemic signs (pulmonary or lymph node involvement).

3. Secondary syphilis — Can produce widespread reddish‑brown papulosquamous plaques on trunk and extremities in older adults; may lack prominent symptoms.

4. Chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus (discoid or subacute cutaneous lupus) — Can present with chronic erythematous plaques that may be hyperpigmented and thickened, especially on sun‑exposed areas.

5. Plaque psoriasis (atypical presentation) — Common cause of chronic reddish plaques; absence of recalled silvery scale makes it less likely but still possible.

Key next steps (to confirm/rule out diagnoses): punch skin biopsy of an active lesion with histopathology and immunophenotyping (including T‑cell receptor gene rearrangement for clonality), fungal stain/PAS; syphilis serology (RPR ± FTA‑ABS); CBC with differential; chest x‑ray (or chest CT) and serum ACE if sarcoidosis suspected; ANA and other autoimmune testing if lupus suspected.
